                         In Levcllaml the night of November 2 conditions were ideal for
        • I   I   o   the formation of hall lightning. For several days the area had been
                      experiencing freak weather, and on the night in question had hccn
                      visited by rain, thunderstorms, nnd li~htuing. Shortly hcfon• the
                      glowing spl1cre upprnachcd the truck, the two m<'n hnd noticed
                      a lightning flash in a ncarhy field. The original description of tlte
                      phenomenon-a ""flaming ball" or n "fiery tonmdo" that floated to-
                      \Vcud and over the truck and detonated with light and heat-fits
                      the classic picture of ball lightning. The truck's engine may have
                      died for one of several reasons. The rain during the evening could
                      hAve seeped under the hood and soaked the ignition or dampened
                      the spnrk plugs. The feed line may have been clogged. Or the region
                      of highly rarefied air created by tbe ball lightning may temporarily
                      have deprived the engine of oxygen.
                         Of the other drivers ncar Levelland that night who reported lmv-
                      ing trouble with balky motors and seeing a blazing object like an
                      egg-shaped fireball, three probably saw baH lightning. Others, after
                      hearing Saucedo·s frightening story, perhaps unconsciously drama-
                      tized their own experiences and magnified ordinary lightning Rashes
                                                                                                                •
                      into attacking fiery objects. It is significant that although the night                   •
                      was stormy, only Saucedo reported seeing the ordinary lightning
                      that normally accompanies a thunderstorm.
                         Since ball lightning is short-Jived and cannot be preserved as
                      tangible evidence, its appearance in Levelland on the night of No-
                      vember 2 can never Le absolutely proved, even though this exp]ana-
                                                                                                I
                                                                                                •
                      tion fits all the facts-facts that in themselves do not warrant so        •
                      lengthy a study. Only the saucer proponents could have converted
                      so trivial a series of events-a few stalled automobiles, halls of flame       •

                      in the sky at the end of thunderstorm-into a national mystery. (Ball
                      lightning doubtless accounts for other UFO reports, such as the phe-
                      nomenon observed at Lock Raven Dam on October 26, 1958, when
                      two men returning late at night from a fishing trip saw a flaming
                      ball hovering above the superstructure of a bridge; it exploded
                                                                                                I
                      with a loud noise and a brilliant white flash and disappeared.)
                         One thing is certain. No evidence exists to suggest the presence
                      of a spaceship O\'er Levelland. Any extraterrestrial vehicle attempt-     I


                      ing to patrol the area that night would certainly have been seen
                      and its path would have been accurately plotted. rvtoonwatch crews
                      in New ~·fexico, Atizona, and Colorado were all watching the skies                    •
                      for a passage of Sputnik, and in Texas itself official observers were
                      on the alert at Big Spring, 100 n1iles southeast of Levelland; at San     I                   -
                      Antonio, 370 miles southeast; at \Vichita Falls, 250 miles east; :tt      I
                                                                                                I
                      Dodson, 162 miles northeast; and at Amarillo, 120 miles north. None       •
                                                                                                I
                      of the trained witnesses at these stations saw anything in the sky        I
                                                                                                I
                      that should not have been there.                                          I
